newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Zaire gets tough on refugees as U.N. envoy arrives.
newsitem.headline: Zaire gets tough on refugees as U.N. envoy arrives.

text.p: Zaire stated categorically it would no longer allow Rwandan and Burundian refugees on its soil as a U.N. envoy arrived on Friday for talks on urgent relief for over a million refugees displaced by fighting.
"No new refugee camps can be built anywhere in Zaire," Information Minister Boguo Makeli declared on state television, reading from decisions of a cabinet meeting.
Most of the existing camps for Hutu refugees who fled to Zaire from Rwanda and Burundi have been abandoned in three weeks of battles between ethnic Tutsis and the army in eastern Zaire.
U.N. envoy Bernard Chretien arrived in Kinshasa on Friday night from Rwanda to pursue talks on a proposed multinational force to help refugees dying in thousands in the bush.

Boguo reiterated Zaire's decision not to allow distribution of food for refugees on its territory, adding: "The movement of refugees in humanitarian corridors must lead from the east to the west -- in other words from Zaire to Rwanda and Burundi."
All relief aid for displaced Zaireans must be landed in the capital Kinshasa, Boguo said in the declaration made shortly after special U.N. envoy Bernard Chretien arrived from Rwanda.
Chretien suggested that the United Nations was not likely to send humanitarian aid into Zaire without some armed force to protect the refugees or relief workers.

"There are tens of thousands of armed men in eastern zaire at the meoment, so it is legitimate for the U.N. to have at least a minimum protection," he told reporters in answer to a question on the subject.
Asked if his negotiations would include immigrant Banyamulenge Tutsis who have seized Zaire's two eastern provinces, the Canadian diplomat said:
"This is a very delicate issue and we'll be discussing it with Zaire."
He said he had received assurances from the Tutsi-led government in Rwanda "that they would use their influence" on the rebels, whom Zaire says are helped by the Rwandan army.

Boguo also announced that the cabinet had ordered the immediate closure until further notice of two college campuses Kinshasa spearheading violent protests against Tutsis and the government of part-Tutsi Prime Minister Kengo wa Dondo.
The army was out in force to block off city streets from a procession of students heading for the funeral of two comrades killed in clashes on Monday with security forces.
Students had planned to disrupt the cabinet meeting but the show of force prevented them, and the highly charged funeral passed off without any incident.
Earlier in Kigali Chretien met Rwanda's president and military chief to try to secure their consent for the deployment of a U.N. force.
He held talks with President Pasteur Bizimungu, a Hutu, and Defence Minister Paul Kagame, the Tutsi widely seen as holding the real power in Rwanda.
The easiest supply routes pass through Rwanda and the rebels who have seized a chunk of eastern Zaire are allies of Kigali.

Rwanda insists the Hutus should come home. Zaire agrees but the refugees, fearing revenge for the 1994 genocide carried out by still-armed militiamen among them, refuse. The Hutu rebels fear they will join 80,000 genocide suspects in Rwandan jails.
